title: Ὄνος καὶ βάτραχοι
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 271. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ὄνος ξύλων γόμον φέρων λίμνην διέβαινεν· ὀλισθὼν δέ, ὡς κατέπεσεν, ἐξαναστῆναι μὴ δυνάμενος ὠδύρετό τε καὶ ἔστενεν.
sentences.tr: Onos xylōn gomon pherōn limnēn diebainen· olisthōn de, hōs katepesen, exanastēnai mē dynamenos ōdyreto te kai estenen.
sentences.l: A donkey carrying a load of wood was crossing a marsh; and having slipped, when he had fallen down, not being able to get up again, he both wailed and groaned.
sentences.i: A donkey was crossing a marsh with a load of wood; he slipped, and when he had gone down he could not get up again, and he wailed and groaned.
sentences.n: λίμνη is standing water — a marshy pool rather than a running stream, which is why the frogs are at home in it. ἐξαναστῆναι is doubly compounded, ἐξ- and ἀνα-, 'to stand up out of' the mud. τε καί couples the two verbs closely: the wailing and the groaning are one performance.

sentences.t: Οἱ δὲ ἐν τῇ λίμνῃ βάτραχοι ἀκούσαντες αὐτοῦ τῶν στεναγμῶν ἔφασαν· « Ὦ οὗτος, καὶ τί ἂν ἐποίησας, εἰ τοσοῦτον ἐνταῦθα χρόνον διέτριβες ὅσον ἡμεῖς, ὅτε πρὸς ὀλίγον πεσὼν οὕτως ὀδύρῃ ; »
sentences.tr: Hoi de en tēi limnēi batrachoi akousantes autou tōn stenagmōn ephasan· « Ō houtos, kai ti an epoiēsas, ei tosouton entautha chronon dietribes hoson hēmeis, hote pros oligon pesōn houtōs odyrēi ; »
sentences.l: And the frogs in the marsh, having heard his groanings, said: « You there, and what would you have done, if you had been spending as much time here as we, when, having fallen for a little, you lament so? »
sentences.i: And the frogs in the marsh heard his groaning and said: « You there — and what would you have done had you been passing as much time here as we do, when a moment's fall sets you lamenting like this? »
sentences.n: The condition is a mixed one: the protasis εἰ … διέτριβες is imperfect and unfulfilled in present time, while ἂν ἐποίησας is aorist and looks to the past. Greek allows the two halves to disagree in time far more freely than English. Ὦ οὗτος is the blunt hailing address, 'you there', used across the collection when one party rounds on another. πρὸς ὀλίγον is 'for a short while' — the ὀλίγον answers τοσοῦτον χρόνον.

sentences.t: Τούτῳ τῷ λόγῳ χρήσαιτο ἄν τις πρὸς ἄνδρα ῥᾴθυμον ἐπ’ ἐλαχίστοις πόνοις δυσφοροῦντα, αὐτὸς τοὺς πλείονας ῥᾳδίως ὑφιστάμενος.
sentences.tr: Toutōi tōi logōi chrēsaito an tis pros andra rhāithymon ep’ elachistois ponois dysphorounta, autos tous pleionas rhāidiōs hyphistamenos.
sentences.l: This story someone might use against a slack man who takes it hard at the smallest labours, being himself one who readily undergoes the greater ones.
sentences.i: This story someone might use against a slack man who makes a grievance of the smallest labours — someone, that is, who shoulders greater ones himself without complaint.
sentences.n: ῥᾴθυμος is the man who takes life easily, slack rather than idle. δυσφορέω ἐπί + dat. is to bear a thing badly, to be put out at it. The final participle ὑφιστάμενος is nominative and so agrees with τις, the person using the story, not with the man it is used against: the reproach only works if the speaker shoulders more himself.
